title: The people of the house
hook: Muslims pray for the Prophet's family in their prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Husayn, chased through a lane and caught. Your line was from me. Which child got your open affection? Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Near the end of the ritual prayer, Muslims sit, and the words get quiet and personal. They bear witness. Then they send blessings on the Prophet. And then, in the words he taught, the blessing widens: on Muhammad, and on the family of Muhammad. A grandson in a lane, a daughter at a mill, a boy beside him on the pulpit: they're folded into the prayer, said again and again across a day. Today: the people of the house.
screen: `SITTING BACK NEAR THE END.` → `BLESSINGS ON THE PROPHET.` → `AND ON THE FAMILY OF MUHAMMAD.`

segments.voice: It starts with a verse. In Pickthall's translation of Surah al-Ahzab: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." The companions knew how to greet him. They didn't know how to ask blessings. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ka'b ibn Ujrah says they asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, exactly that. And he taught them a form that begins, in Arabic, Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, wa ala ali Muhammad: O God, send blessings on Muhammad, and on the family of Muhammad, as you sent blessings on Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. So the family was in the answer from the start. The phrase ahl al-bayt, the people of the house, comes from the same surah. Pickthall renders it "O Folk of the Household", in a verse that speaks of God wishing to remove uncleanness from them. Who is the household? Here Muslims answer in different ways. In Sahih Muslim, Aisha tells of a morning the Prophet came out wearing a cloak, and drew under it Hasan, Husayn, Fatimah and Ali, and recited that verse. Shi'a Muslims hold that these, the people of the cloak, are the household the verse means, with a special and lasting place in guiding the community. Sunni readings include the people of the cloak and also the Prophet's wives, since the verse sits among words addressed to them, and some widen it to his clan. Both love them. Both say their names with honor. And in both, the blessing in the prayer never stops at one name. It goes on: and on his family.
screen: `ASK BLESSINGS ON HIM.` · `HOW? AND ON THE FAMILY OF MUHAMMAD.` · `O FOLK OF THE HOUSEHOLD.` · `WHO IS THE HOUSEHOLD? TWO ANSWERS.` · then, large: `AHL AL-BAYT: THE PEOPLE OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: This ends our days on the family: Fatimah, her hands, Hasan and Husayn, and the house they lived in. Now the practice. Sit, and breathe. Let the faces of this week come one by one. A daughter at the mill. A boy on the pulpit. A boy in the lane. If you pray, you can say the blessing he taught, slowly: Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, wa ala ali Muhammad. Say it a few times, and let the second half land. If you don't pray, just hold the picture of one household, remembered with love. The bell holds the time.
Ahl al-bayt. The people of the house: the Prophet's household, blessed with him in the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: and on his family. Today, when you thank or praise someone, add their family to it: and your mother, and your kids. Watch what it does. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims say the salawat, the blessing on the Prophet and his family, in the sitting near the end of the ritual prayer, and often at other times when his name is mentioned; in some gatherings it is said aloud together.

original.note: Arabic: the people of the house, the Prophet's household (Qur'an 33:33).

trapdoor: what you thought: a phrase for the Prophet's relatives.
what it means: the household blessed with him in the prayer he taught: and on the family of Muhammad.
what a scholar hears: the term comes from 33:33; Muslim's report of the cloak names Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn, and Sunni and Shi'a scholars draw the circle in different ways.
recall: listed the good he had done

notes: Index hook says 'every Muslim prays for the Prophet's family in each prayer'; softened under the claims rule to the sitting near the end of the prayer. Note that the salawat's ruling in the final sitting varies by school.
Pickthall 33:56 and the phrase 'O Folk of the Household' in 33:33: confirm exact wording.
Bukhari 3370 and Muslim 2424 numbering and paraphrase: confirm.
Sunni and Shi'a views of who the household is: summarized without ranking; confirm both are fair, including 'some widen it to his clan'.
The salawat is quoted in Arabic transliteration as the form taught in the hadith (not a new prayer); confirm the transliteration.
Day 822 closes the part 'The family' (818–822); the practice says so.
